column4: The section defines tasbīḥ as declaring God free of every evil and sets true divine highness against self-claimed grandeur; this verse glorifies and exalts God far above what they say, including their claim of great elevation.
The section’s tasbīḥ gloss is God’s purification from every evil; this closing command glorifies the Lord of might above what they attribute, locating true majesty in God.
The section says the name identifies its bearer and raises the named one’s mention; this verse assigns the most beautiful names to God and commands calling on Him by them.
The section joins the Lord’s name to exaltation and honor; this verse blesses the name of the Lord who possesses majesty and honor, making the name itself the site of that reverence.
The section places the Lord’s name at the center of glorification; this verse permits calling God or the Most Merciful and says the most beautiful names belong to Him.
The section’s first image glorifies the Lord’s name; this verse identifies God as the sole deity and says the most beautiful names are His, specifying the bearer of the names.

The section’s k-b-r gloss includes magnifying God with the takbīr; this command praises God as having no child or partner and calls for magnifying Him greatly, directing grandeur to its proper bearer.
The section ties al-aʿlā to the Creator; this verse says God originates and repeats creation and that the highest attribute belongs to Him in the heavens and earth.

The section’s d-n-w gloss includes what is low or lesser, and its central choice is the lower life over the better Hereafter; this verse uses “أدنى” for the inferior thing chosen in place of what is better, a concrete but worldly-food instance of that lower-for-better exchange.

The section contrasts the high with the low or near; this verse calls the nearest heaven “السماء الدنيا,” giving that low/near pole a literal place in the sky and contrasting it with the section’s highest heavens.
The section’s d-n-w gloss includes the nearer thing and its ʿ-l-w axis the highest; this verse names the nearest heaven and describes its adornment, making the same vertical scale cosmic.
The section’s low/near and high poles can describe the sky as well as worldly life; this verse specifically calls the adorned heaven the nearest one, a spatial use of “الدنيا.”

The section’s d-n-w dictionary gloss includes what is nearest; this verse locates the Romans’ defeat in the nearest land, preserving that spatial sense of the root apart from the moral choice of worldly life.

The section’s s-m-w dictionary branch evokes the crescent becoming visible above the horizon; this verse says the moon has measured phases, giving the crescent a place in the recurring lunar cycle and its timekeeping use.

The section’s s-m-w branch names the crescent rising above the horizon; this verse swears by the moon when full, a later visible phase that completes the crescent’s growth rather than repeating the crescent itself.
The section warns that highness can become self-exaltation; this verse says Iblis was arrogant and among the disbelievers, identifying the refusal behind a false claim to rank.

The section distinguishes granted divine highness from self-claimed grandeur; God asks Iblis whether he was arrogant or among the exalted, making the claim to rank the issue of the command to prostrate.
The section’s axis exposes self-awarded superiority; this neighbor gives Iblis’s reason for refusing, his claim that he is better because he was created from fire while Adam was created from clay.
The section links corrupted height to arrogance; Iblis answers the command to prostrate by claiming he is better than Adam, a direct self-ranking rather than bestowed elevation.
The section warns that ʿ-l-w can turn into self-exaltation; God rebukes Iblis’s arrogance and orders him to descend, making the high/low reversal explicit.

The section’s k-b-r family distinguishes divine greatness from a creature’s self-importance; this verse says Iblis refused and grew arrogant, the original scene of a creature resisting God’s command through claimed rank.

The section’s ʿ-l-w gloss says a ruler’s rising in the land can mean tyranny and self-magnification; this verse says Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and divided its people, giving that corruption its political scene.

The section connects false highness with Pharaoh; after Moses and Aaron bring clear signs, this verse says Pharaoh and his chiefs were arrogant, a repeated account of resistance to divinely backed truth.
The section’s image opposes true highness to a ruler’s self-claimed supremacy; Pharaoh boasts of his kingdom and the rivers beneath him, grounding his status claim in worldly dominion.
The section presents Pharaoh as claiming the highest place; this neighbor completes his boast by belittling Moses as insignificant and barely able to make himself clear.

The section’s ʿ-l-w gloss warns of arrogant rising on earth; this verse says God turns away from His signs those who act arrogantly in the land, a direct boundary between self-exaltation and receiving guidance.

The section contrasts a ruler’s earthly self-exaltation with genuine elevation; this verse says heaven’s gates will not open to those who deny God’s signs and act arrogantly, setting a boundary on their claimed ascent.
The section makes al-aʿlā the image of elevation; this verse says God raised Idris to a high station, showing rank as something bestowed rather than claimed.

The section contrasts Pharaoh’s claimed highness with true rank; this verse says God made people successors and raised some above others in degrees as a test, presenting elevation as assigned and accountable.

The section says the near worldly life is surpassed by what is better and more enduring; this verse calls wealth and children adornments of worldly life, but says enduring good deeds are better with the Lord for reward and hope.

The section says the Hereafter is better and more enduring than the low worldly life; this verse contrasts what people possess and what is with God, saying the former ends while what is with God remains.

The section defines worldly life as low and near against the Hereafter; this verse directs people to seek the Hereafter with what God has given them while not forgetting their share of this world, qualifying how the lower life may be used.
The section says the worldly life is the lower choice beside what lasts; this verse describes people rejoicing in worldly life and calls its enjoyment small compared with the Hereafter.
The section names the choice of the low worldly life; this verse describes those who desire the present life and its adornment, connecting that preference to deeds done for its reward.
The section says the Hereafter is better and more enduring than worldly life; this neighbor completes 11:15 by saying what its seekers gain there and that they have no share in the Hereafter.

The section contrasts remembrance of the Lord with preferring the low worldly life; this verse warns against following someone whose heart is heedless of remembrance and who follows desire, a specific opposite stance to the one who fears and remembers.
The section links remembrance of the Lord’s name with prayer and glorification; this command to believers to remember God much repeats the remembrance side of that pairing.
The section joins remembrance to glorifying the Lord; this neighbor completes 33:41 by commanding glorification morning and evening, giving the paired acts a daily rhythm.

The section places God’s true highness above a creature’s self-claim; this verse rebukes people for failing to appraise God properly and depicts the earth held in His grasp and the heavens folded, setting divine scale beyond human grandeur.
The section’s tasbīḥ gloss is to declare God free of every evil; this verse denies God a child or partner and declares Him above what they describe, making that purification specific.
The section defines tasbīḥ as declaring God above every evil; this verse announces God’s command and glorifies Him above what they associate with Him, a direct instance of that act.

The section assigns true highness to God and exposes self-claimed grandeur; this verse says the highest description belongs to God, setting divine measure against the deficient example it attributes to those who deny the Hereafter.
